Timeline::repeat¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Timeline Timeline::repeat(std::int64_t times) const

Tile Complete Temporal Blocks¶

repeat() copies the complete receiver block times times along axis 0. It is block tiling, not element-by-element duplication. For [A, B], repeat(2) is [A, B, A, B], not [A, A, B, B].

For a non-scalar shape [n, d1, ..., dk], the result shape is [n * times, d1, ..., dk]. Trailing dimensions identify one record’s geometry and remain unchanged. A scalar is promoted to shape [1] before repetition, so even scalar.repeat(1) returns a one-element vector.

times

Result

0

Empty axis 0 with trailing dimensions preserved

1

One materialized block; scalar shape becomes [1]

Greater than 1

Blocks appear consecutively in receiver order

Negative

Rejected

Example 1. The vector example makes block order visible.

const auto row = pluss::timeline::date({"2024-01-01", "2024-01-02"});
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(row.repeat(2)) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[4], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-02 00:00:00, 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]

Higher-Rank Shape Preservation¶

For matrices and 3-D timelines, repetition copies axis-0 slices. It never flattens the source and never repeats independently along a trailing axis.

Example 2. Repeating one matrix row twice produces two rows with the same two columns.

const auto matrix = pluss::timeline::date({{"2024-01-01", "2024-01-02"}});
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(matrix.repeat(2)) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2, 2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]

Logical Order And Ownership¶

The receiver may be strided. repeat() first follows logical indices, so padding or skipped allocation positions are never copied into the result. The result is newly allocated contiguous storage, retains the receiver’s timezone, and preserves NaT at every repeated position.

Time and payload storage are proportional to numel() * times. This is a real copy, not a broadcasted view; use it when independent materialized records are required.

Example 3. A stride-two source still repeats dates 1 and 2 in logical order.

std::array<std::int64_t, 4> backing{
    1'704'067'200'000'000'000LL, 11,
    1'704'153'600'000'000'000LL, 22};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> shape{2};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> strides{2};
const auto strided = pluss::Timeline::from_buffer(
    backing.data(), shape, strides, {}, "UTC");
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(strided.repeat(2)) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[4], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-02 00:00:00, 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]

Scalar Promotion And Zero Repetitions¶

Scalar promotion gives record-oriented code one uniform result rank. Zero repetitions uses the same geometry as empty_like(): axis 0 is zero and all trailing dimensions survive.

Example 4. A scalar repeated once becomes [1]; a [1,2] matrix repeated zero times becomes [0,2].

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(
    pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-01").repeat(1)) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(matrix.repeat(0)) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[1], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00 ]
Timeline(shape=[0, 2], tz=UTC)

Validation And Range Safety¶

times must be non-negative. Before allocation, repeat() checks both the axis-0 multiplication and the total element-count multiplication. A request whose shape or storage size cannot be represented is rejected rather than wrapping into a smaller allocation.

Example 5. Negative and overflowing counts fail before producing a result.

try {
  (void)row.repeat(-1);
} catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "rejected\n"; }
try {
  (void)row.repeat(std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::max());
} catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "rejected\n"; }

Output¶

rejected
rejected
